docs.text: IBM Bob Level 3 i. What is IBM Bob? IBM Bob is an AI-powered partner for the entire software development lifecycle (SDLC) , and it lives where your developers already work: inside the development environment itself. It is tempting to file Bob alongside the many code-completion assistants that have flooded the marketplace since LLMs arrived — but that comparison sells it short. Bob is not simply a code generator, but a partner for every step in your weekly workflow (for developers and sellers, alike.) A code generator helps at the exact point in time that a function gets written. Bob is built to help across the whole arc of a project: planning a feature before a line of code exists, reasoning about an unfamiliar codebase, implementing changes, and automating the repetitive work that surrounds real development. A WORD ON WORKING WITH GENERATIVE AI IBM Bob is powered by generative AI and LLMs, and a defining trait of these systems is that they are non-deterministic — unlike the deterministic tools most developers are accustomed to. In practice, that means the same prompt can produce different code from one run to the next. This is both a strength and a quirk of the technology, and it is something to work with rather than against. Precision is what tips the odds in your favor. The more clearly you describe what you want, the more closely Bob's output will mirror your intent; conversely, the smallest change in wording can meaningfully change the generated code. Throughout this lab, your results may differ from the solutions shown — and that is expected, not a defect. Whenever an output diverges, you have three good options: refine the prompt and try again, edit the generated code by hand, or simply proceed if the variation still compiles and runs. Human review remains essential at every step, and never more so than while you are still learning the tool. At its core, Bob does three things exceptionally well: Writes and modifies code across an entire codebase, from natural language instructions Understands codebases by reading and reasoning about complex project structures, dependencies, and architectural patterns Automates the busy-work of development: from documentation, to commit messages, to test scaffolding ii. Bob across the software development lifecycle A distinction worth holding onto is scope . Where a traditional AI assistant is anchored to the moment of writing or fixing code, Bob is designed to support the lifecycle around it — helping you plan features before implementation begins, understand the full context of a project before making changes, and keep the developer in control at every step. Bob augments the way your teams already work; it does not replace their judgment. Keep ahold of that last point as you work your way through the remainder of the hands-on material, as it is the thread that weaves together so many of Bob's strengths and its value to IBM clients. iii. Where Bob meets you: the IDE and the Shell Bob comes in two form factors to meet developers wherever they are most productive: Interface Description Bob IDE A VS Code extension providing an agentic sidebar, inline code assistance, and mode-based interaction Bob Shell A terminal-based interface offering the same capabilities in a keyboard-driven, automation-friendly form You will spend most of this course in the Bob IDE, where the Visual Studio Code-like user interface of the Bob IDE will already feel at-home to many developers and users. In the final module of the hands-on lab, you'll have the opportunity to briefly touch upon the Bob Shell interface — where you will find that everything learned up to that point also applies programatically as well. iv. Curriculum: AI-assisted code maturity curve The four modules constituting the hands-on work ahead trace the AI-assisted code maturity curve — and as you shift right along it, you will progressively hand Bob more responsibility, with Bob earning that trust by keeping you (the human) in command the entire way. Module Stage What it means for your developers — and your clients 1 Assist Bob accelerates everyday work in the editor, and you accept or reject every change. Velocity from day one with near-zero risk. 2 Delegate Bob takes a whole feature from idea to working code, but builds only what you've reviewed and approved first. 3 Tailor Bob learns your codebase, enforces your standards, and adapts to each role, so it behaves like a teammate who already knows how you work. 4 Scale & Extend Bob stays reliable on large, long-running work and plugs into the tools your enterprise already runs. A core, unifying theme of the journey you're embarking upon: the developer always stays in control. At the Assist stage, control is regulated as you choose to accept (or reject) each generative AI-suggested code recommendation, keystroke by keystroke. Within the Delegate module, control is maintained through approval of Bob-generated plans before a single line of AI-generated code is written. At Tailor , it means encoding the very rules Bob must adhere to. Within the Scale & Extend module, it means governing context, credentials, and tool access. As you and Bob together progress right along the maturity curve, capabilities will expand as trust grows. That escalation is the story — and it is the story your sellers can carry into a C-suite conversation: not "here are some features," but "here is how your teams grow into an AI partner without losing agency to an AI agent." v. Environment: Galaxium Travels Watch first: Chapter 1: Demo Application: Galaxium Travels [IBM Bob L3] Maximilian Jesch (Outbound Product Manager — IBM Bob) walks through the demo scenario that ties the hands-on modules together. [2 min] For the purposes of the hands-on materials and your untaking in building trust with IBM Bob, you'll be making use of the Galaxium Travels application and code base: a fictional, luxury space-travel booking system whose source code is publicly available on GitHub. Rather than show Bob as throwaway snippets and discrete feature demonstration, it's important to realize the full end-to-end journey that a customer will experience in working with the service. Therefore, this hands-on material will put you to work using a unified, production-style codebase from start to finish. It is the consistent backdrop against which each stage of the AI maturity curve comes to life. Galaxium Travels follows a familiar full-stack shape: Frontend: React and TypeScript Backend: Python, exposing both REST and MCP interfaces Database: SQLite, with seed data for development and testing The backend is organized around a SQLite database containing the domain's data models (flights, users, bookings), the schemas that validate them, and seed data to work with. It exposes the application two ways: A REST API of standard HTTP endpoints for the frontend and other clients A Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface that allows Bob to interact as a tool with the backend directly A local API browser is also available so that you can exercise endpoints (retrieving flights, registering users, making bookings) without needing to traverse the frontend application. The React/TypeScript frontend, for its part, connects to those same REST endpoints and mimics the experience that an end user (consumer of the luxury travel service) would see: browsing available flights, registering and signing in, and booking a seat. As you move through the curriculum, you will continuously add new features to the application. The order of operations in adding these new capabilities is iterative and deliberate, with each building on the features of the previous function: Email validation — Module 1.1, Next Edit Prediction Retry logic for API calls — Module 1.2, Literate Coding Seat-class tiers (Economy, Business, Galaxium) — Module 2, the Agentic Sidebar vi. Should you wish to fully explore the source code yourself, it is publicly available and supported on GitHub. docs.text: MODULE 1 | ASSIST TAB COMPLETION & NEXT EDIT PREDICTION i. Bob in your workflow This is the first (and most gentle) stage of the AI maturity curve, and therefore a natural sweet spot for building your understanding of IBM Bob. Across this module, you'll work shoulder to shoulder with Bob from the perspective of a software developer paired with the Bob editor. As you work, Bob will be anticipating the next keystroke, drafting the next few lines, and making targeted edits upon your request — all the while keeping the developer ( you ) in control of accepting or rejecting every AI-generated proposed change. The value that IBM Bob provides in this will be apparenty right from the onset: teams can move faster without breaking their train of thought, and nothing lands in the codebase that they did not explicitly choose to include. It is the most logical on-ramp to working with an AI partner, and it pays off from the very first session. Watch first: Chapter 2.1: Next Edit Prediction and Tab Completion [IBM Bob L3] Maximilian Jesch (Outbound Product Manager — IBM Bob) demonstrates Bob's tab completion and next edit predictions. [1 min] ii. Why this matters The quickest way to lose a developer's confidence in an AI tool is to pull them out of their workflow. Bob's first two capabilities are designed to do precisely the opposite: it keeps a developer in the work, while quietly removing friction from the process. These two features are: Tab completion Next edit prediction The two capabilities operate as a unified pair: the first suggests code from context; the second anticipates where you will need to go next. How tab completion works Tab completion is a familiar idea executed unusually well. Where conventional autocomplete reacts to the few characters you have just typed, Bob reads the surrounding context to make a genuinely informed suggestion — drawing on the comments describing your intent, the patterns and structure already present in the code, your project's conventions and style, and related code in other files. The result feels less like word-completion and more like a colleague finishing your thought. Accepting suggestions When Bob offers a suggestion, the human in the loop retains control and has the last word on what is implemented: Press Tab to accept it Keep typing to override the AI-generated suggestions Watch it update dynamically as you continue your train of thought Next edit predictions Real code changes are rarely confined to a single line within the codebase. Add a new field or variable to the code, and you'll oftentime find yourself needing to use it again elsewhere; introduce a function, and something downstream will need to call it. Next edit prediction is built around that practical reality: after you accept an AI-generated suggestion, Bob anticipates the related edit you are likely to need as a follow-up and moves you there. You can conceptualize this as a rhythm between the developer and their AI partner. The developer describes what they want in a comment, allows Bob to suggest the code fix, presses Tab to accept the suggestion, and presses Tab again to jump to the next predicted location — where Bob positions the cursor exactly where the new code needs to be invoked. iii. Hands-on: adding email validation with Next Edit Prediction Follow the video for a full walkthrough of this scenario: Chapter 2.1: Next Edit Prediction and Tab Completion [IBM Bob L3] EXPECT SOME VARIABILITY Generative AI is non-deterministic and as such your results may differ from what you see here. If an output diverges, consider further refining the prompt, following up with another prompt, or adjusting the code by hand. Iteration and further precision are often the best remedies. Let's begin by adding to Galaxium Travels ' set of capabilities a new feature that's currently missing: validation of email addresses that a user types when they sign in. In the Visual Studio Code (VS Code) activity bar, click Explorer . Click Open Folder . From the File Explorer view, highlight the galaxium-travels folder and select the folder. Drill down into galaxium-travels folder contents and locate the UserIdentification.tsx file. It will be nestled inside the following directory hierarchy: Filepath: / booking_system_frontend / src / components / user / UserIdentification.tsx Double-click on UserIdentification.tsx to open the contents within the IDE. Navigate to the UserIdentification function ( line 19 of UserIdentification.tsx ). In order to demonstrate IBM Bob's ability to generate functional application code based on basic, natural language specifications, we'll begin with a simple one-liner comment that describes the work we'd like the application to perform. In this example, that will be validation of email addresses to ensure that users signing up for the Galaxium service are supplying compliant email addresses that follow the expected formatting. Begin by moving the cursor to line 19 of the file (within the UserIdentification function) and type the following, including the forward-slash ( / ) characters: //validate email addresses Then add a blank (empty) line before and after this commented line. The result should appear as the following: UserIdentification.tsx 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(false); const [isNewUser, setIsNewUser] = useState(false); //validate email addresses const handleSubmit = async (e: React.FormEvent) => { e.preventDefaut(); } Move your cursor to the end of the newly-created //validate email addresses comment on line 19 , then press Enter followed by Tab to invoke Bob's Tab Completion feature. Tab Completion will immediately insert greyed-out, italicized text — this represents the AI-suggested code completion based on the natural language "validate email addresses" comment. At this stage, the code suggestion is still only a suggestion: you, as the operator at the helm, have the option to: accept; modify; or reject and move on. Press the Tab key once again to accept the suggested code. Note that the grey italics are replaced by normal characters after accepting the suggestion. This denotes that the AI-suggested code has been committed to your file as working code. As a reminder, because Bob's suggestions are non-deterministic, your generated function may look slightly different from the code documented. If the generated code does not compile, first compare the inserted function with the example shown in the lab documentation. You may either manually correct the function by hand to make the documented solution, or delete the generated code and repeat the prediction step (using Tab as before) again. Now let's return to the Galaxium Travels web app and confirm the change took effect. To do so, you will first need to reboot the web app service. To open a Terminal window, click the Terminal button at the bottom-center portion of the Bob IDE interface or navigate using the top menu bar into Terminal > New Terminal (which will open a fresh Terminal screen at the bottom-center portion of the UI). Within the Terminal window, locate and click the + icon, along the right-hand side of the Terminal window. This will launch a new Terminal connection into which you will next input additional commands. The commands to be issued to the Terminal console depending on the operating system your machine is running upon. From the expandable options below, follow and execute the instructions aligned to your machine's OS (either Mac/Linux or Windows). After completing the instructions within the appropriate tab, proceed to the next step in the lab guide. MAC OR LINUX On macOS or Linux, run the following commands one at a time. Step 1: cd \~ /galaxium-travels Step 2: ./start.sh You should see a "Galaxium Travels is running!" prompt returned to the console (amongst other messages) once the application has deployed successfully. WINDOWS OS On Windows, run the following commands one at a time. Step 1: cd $HOME \g alaxium-travels Step 2: cd booking_system_backend Step 3: python -m venv .venv Step 4: .venv \S cripts \a ctivate Step 5: python server.py DO NOT CLOSE THE TERMINAL WINDOW For the following Steps 6-9 , you will be required to open a second Terminal window. Do not close the Terminal previously used for Steps 1-5 . This window will need to remain open and active for the duration of the lab. Step 6: After having completed all of Steps 1-5 , open a new Terminal window by pressing the Plus button. Step 7: Within the new Terminal window, execute the following commands one-by-one in sequence: cd $HOME\galaxium-travels Step 8: cd booking_system_frontend Step 9: npm run dev You should see a "Galaxium Travels is running!" prompt returned to the console (amongst other messages) once the application has deployed successfully. Open a web browser on your local machine and visit the following URL to access the Galaxium Travels application: WEB BROWSER http://localhost:5173/ Once the Galaxium Travels site has loaded, click on Flights . Click the Book Now button under any of the listed flights to test its functionality. The web page will redirect to a Sign In panel. From this panel, we will be able to confirm (or troubleshoot) that the Bob-suggested email validation functionality is performing its intended job. Within the Name field, supply a name of your choosing. Within the Email field, try any combination of improperly formatted text that you like. Remember: you want to test that the tool is rejecting any inputs that don't match a standard email address. You can even test with a random string of characters like $$$$$ , as an example. The expected behavior of the function should be to reject any inproper addresses ( $$$$$ ) and accept a standard address ( bienko@ibm.com ).

But much of a developer's day is spent making precise, surgical change to code that already exists. To that end, literate coding is the tool of choice. It lets you annotate— using plain, natural language instructions — direct inside of a file where you needed the changes to occur. Bob then takes care of the heavy lifting by ensuring that every change is accounted for and that no instructions are missed. IBM Bob reads the instruction in place and produces a targeted, localized modification. Once active, it allows those users to write natural-language instructions at a precise code location. They can target the exact section of code where changes are to be made; alternatively, they can queue up several instructions in sequence, across multiple locations of a single file. docs.text: MODULE 2 | DELEGATE THE AGENTIC SIDEBAR i. From assistant to partner In the previous Assist module, you engaged with IBM Bob in its most "manual" and "hands-on" form: it finished lines of code for you, predicted the next set of edits to be performed, and made surgical changes (with your approval) sequentially throughout a codebase. From the end-user (your) perspective, the experience thus far has felt closely watched and tightly chaperoned. Every action Bob has taken has been directly instrumented by you, or at the very least required your direct sign-off at every step in the sequence, to ensure no changes were made to the code base without your expressed permission. AI MATURITY CURVE This makes sense when viewed through the lens of the AI Maturity Curve that was discussed previously. Where you are currently in your journey with IBM Bob— progressing from the nascent Assist stage on the left-most portion of the curve, moving further to the right into the Delegate phase —is at a point where trust in the AI technology should be low. Coordinating code changes with IBM Bob with a healthy degree of skepticism is a valid way to safely vet the AI partner's capabilities, build trust in its ability to deliver the results you seek, and gradually begin delegating more responsibility to that agent. The Delegate module ahead raises those stakes considerably and asks for a much higher degree of trust on the user's (your) part. The work ahead will transform your perspective of IBM Bob from an assistant into a trusted partner. To earn that trust, Bob will demonstrate taking an entire feature of the Galaxium travel app— one that spans the frontend, the backend, and the database —and shephard it from idea to working code , largely on its own. The reason delegation of this magnitude remains safe— and why you should feel confident in demonstrating this to even a cautious or skeptical prospective enterprise audience —is the core discipline of IBM Bob that was introduced earlier, and will be reinforced here: Bob builds only what you have reviewed and approved in a plan first . Human control does not degrade as the stakes rise. Control remains anchored from the start of the process and at the onset of the AI Maturity Curve, with the plan of execution you establish for Bob, your AI partner. ii. Why this matters Watch first: Chapter 2.3: The Agentic Sidebar [IBM Bob L3] Maximilian Jesch (Outbound Product Manager — IBM Bob) showcases how to work with Bob's agentic chat. [5 min] All work you have performed across the hands-on lab so far has been inline coding modifications: IBM Bob performing work at the exact spot your cursor sits. Bob's Agentic Sidebar functionality is a different proposition altogether. It is the primary interface for complex, multi-step work. It also enables Bob to: Read through files Reason across entire codebases Ask clarifying questions in follow-up to user prompts Implement a requested feature end-to-end. iii. The Agentic Sidebar Where the Next Edit Prediction and Literate Coding assist functionality that was showcased in the previous module required your direct input— keystroke by keystroke —the Agentic Sidebar allows you hand over and delegate entire objectives (and very complex workflows) with a single request. It is the most productive way to work with Bob. The point at which you have sufficient trust and confidence in Bob to faithfully execute this work is where the AI partnership truly begins, further progressing you along the AI Maturity Curve journey. UNDERSTANDING THE VARIOUS MODES The agentic sidebar offers several modes , each tuned for a specific phase of development and code lifecycle management. For substantial feature work, the recommended workflow is a deliberate sequence: Plan mode → review → new conversation → Code mode Each step of this sequence (from plan, review, converse, and code) exists deliberately as part of a methodical workflow. Before going hands-on with the agentic sidebar, it's worth taking a moment first to explore the "sweet spot" use cases for each mode. iv. Plan Mode THINK BEFORE BUILDING Plan mode is the starting point for any feature or architectural change of consequence. In this mode Bob has read-only access to the codebase — it cannot change anything — and its sole job is to produce a detailed plan before a single line of code is written. Reach for it whenever a change touches multiple files or layers, when you are designing new components or data models, or when you simply want to understand the scope of a change before committing to it. Entering it is straightforward: open the agentic sidebar in VS Code, select Plan from the mode selector, and describe the feature in natural language. From there, Bob reads the relevant files to understand the existing structure, asks clarifying questions to resolve ambiguity before planning, and then generates planning documents — typically two: an implementation plan (a detailed specification of what the feature does, how it will be built, how it will be tested, and how it should behave — often 100 to 200-plus lines) and an architecture plan (a higher-level account of structural decisions, component interactions, and data flow). These documents are saved to the project and become the authoritative specification for the build. v. Review and Plan A DEVELOPER'S RESPONSIBILITY The review and planning process is at the core of everything you (the user) performs with the service. The plans that IBM Bob generates are not loose suggestions — they are exactly what Bob will build, verbatim. Approving a plan you have not adequately reviewed or read ahead of time will hand full responsibility for any misaligned or incorrect implementation squarely to you . Bob, as they say, was only following orders. Before you proceed with delegating tasks to Bob, it's imperative that you read both the implementation plan and the architecture plan in full. Verify that the described behavior matches the feature you intended. Confirm that the testing requirements make sense. Correct any misunderstanding now, by revising your prompt or asking a follow-up, while correction is cheap (and far less costly a fix than after post-implementation.) RESPONSIBILITY AS A DEVELOPER AND END-USER Read the plans. To re-emphasize (and this is true across all LLMs): human-in-the-loop review is the single most important quality gate in any agentic workflow. The quality of the final implementation is directly tied to the quality of the plan you approve. vi. Code Mode IMPLEMENT APPROVED PLANS In Code mode , Bob has full access to file operations and command execution. It can create, modify, and run code across an entire codebase. Once the plan is reviewed and approved, the implementation happens withinin a new conversation . That detail is not incidental. Starting fresh clears Bob's context window, which keeps the implementation focused, prevents the earlier planning discussion from eating into the token budget, and reduces the chance of Bob conflating strategizing plans with implementing instructions. To carry the specification into the new conversation, you will need to reference the planning documents with context mentions. For example, the following two paths specify contextual details about a (hypothethical) implementation and architecture plan. @/path/to/implementation-plan.md @/path/to/architecture-plan.md The process for "switching" into Code mode is straightforward and simple— and you'll have the opportunity to practice this yourself in the following hands-on steps — for reference: Start a new conversation Select Code from the mode selector Optionally reference any relevant planning documents or context with @/path/to/file Send the implementation request to Bob, which will carry out the task vii. Auto-Approval CONTROL, DIALED TO TASTE By default, Bob will ask for permission before performing consequential actions such as writing files, running Terminal commands, or executing tests. The auto-approval setting governs whether those actions proceed automatically or pause for your review, with various configurations you can set to determine the level of autonomy (and trust) you are comfortable delegating to Bob. Setting Behavior When to use Manual approval Every action requires explicit confirmation Sensitive codebases, unfamiliar tasks Auto-approve Bob proceeds without interruption Controlled demos, trusted environments Hybrid Auto-approve low-risk actions; prompt for riskier ones Day-to-day development The convenience of full auto-approval comes at the trade-off of escalating exposure risk. If autonomy is dialed up to the highest degree, Bob will be able to run arbitrary Terminal commands without human review — reducing the management overhead on human users, but potentially introducing mistakes into a plan that can propagate unchecked. For most work, a hybrid and balanced posture is the sensible default — auto-approve file reads and writes, but require confirmation before command execution. Set auto-approval in Bob's settings panel according to the sensitivity of the project and the trust you place in the approved plan. viii. Referencing files CONTEXTUALIZED MENTIONS When you point Bob at files in the sidebar, use context mentions rather than copying and pasting their contents: Mention syntax Effect @/path/to/file.js Includes the full contents of a specific file @/path/to/folder Includes all files within a directory @problems Includes current VS Code Problems panel diagnostics @terminal Includes recent terminal output Mentions are resolved at the moment you send the message, giving Bob precise, targeted information without burning context on unrelated files. ix. Key takeaways The agentic sidebar is Bob's most capable interface for complex, multi-file features. Always begin substantial work in Plan mode to define a specification before any code is written. Read the generated plans in full , as these define exactly what Bob will build. Start a new conversation before switching to Code mode, to keep the context window clean and focused. Use context mentions ( @/path/to/file ) to carry the planning documents into the implementation conversation. Set auto-approval deliberately, according to the sensitivity of the project and the complexity of the task. Plan → review → new conversation → Code is the standard pattern for feature development with Bob and a discipline that ensures AI delegation remains safe. In the following section, you will apply this deeper understanding of the agentic sidebar using Bob to further enrich the Galaxium Travels application.

docs.text: MODULE 4 | SCALE & EXTEND THE CONTEXT WINDOW i. Keeping Bob reliable at scale Across this module, you will first look under the hood at the context window mechanics that make Bob tick. Arguably, the context window might be the single biggest factor in keeping Bob's output at the highest quality across the most ambitious tasks. The habits and best practices that developers (you) adopt in maximizing the utility of this resource can have tremendous impacts on the quality of work that Bob is able to perform. Afterwards, you'll take Bob out of the IDE entirely and into the Terminal console: Bob Shell . This programmatic interface for Bob unlocks automation, scripting, and parallelized workstreams. Finally, you will experiment with connecting Bob to your existing systems through Model Context Protocol (MCP) , the open source standard that lets Bob interact directly with the external tools your teams use daily. Governance remains paramount at this stage. As the human-in-the-loop and final arbiter of control, you must decide what context Bob carries, what credentials it holds, and which tools it is permissioned to reach. Watch first: Chapter 4.1: Context Window [IBM Bob L3] Maximilian Jesch (Outbound Product Manager — IBM Bob) digs into the details of Bob's context window. [4 min] AI MATURITY CURVE By the end of Module 3 | Tailor , IBM Bob knew nearly every facet about your project, adhered to your organization's coding standards, and had adapted itself to each role on your team — and all of that was committed to the repository, shared, and automatically enforced. The final stage along the AI Maturity Curve journey reflects the two things that separate a promising demo from a dependable enterprise partner : staying reliable on the largest, longest-running workloads; ultimately, connecting to everything else that your organization already runs today. In other words, addressing the enterprise challenges of Scale and Extensibility . ii. Why this matters The context window represents the total amount of information a large language model (LLM) can hold "in mind" during a single session or conversation. It is also sets the potential limit of how much work any given LLM can perform: the larger the context window, the more substantial scale of task that can be performed (and likely the higher quality output that can be achieved.) Understanding how a context window "fills" (and how to manage these finite resources effectively) is what separates a polished technology demonstration from one that degrades in quality halfway through the work. This lesson is conceptual. There are no steps to run, but the habits it instills will shape every other interaction you have with Bob. In the following chapter, you will go hands-on once again and put this theory in practice. iii. What is a context window? The models powering Bob offer a context window of 200,000 tokens — roughly 150,000 words , about the length of The Fellowship of the Ring . Every conversation begins with that full capacity available, and it holds everything : instructions, file contents, conversation history, and Bob's own responses. Once the window fills, the oldest content within the context window has to either be dropped from memory or summarized to make room. At the start of every conversation, content loads in a predictable sequence: ORDER OF OPERATIONS CONTENT NOTES 1 Bob system prompt Hidden from the user; contains Bob's core instructions 2 Mode description The definition of the currently active Bob Mode ( Code , Plan , Custom , etc.) 3 Rules Content from all files in .bob/rules/ 4 MCP tool definitions Can be very large, depending on the number and complexity of connected MCP servers 5 Conversation messages User prompts and Bob's responses 6 File reads and writes Contents of files Bob reads or produces during the conversation THE IMPORTANCE OF GOVERNANCE MCP tool definitions deserve special attention. The more external servers connected via MCP to Bob, the more rapidly that a significant slice of Bob's context window is exhausted before the user (you) send even a single message. This is why the importance of good governance and planning are emphasized again and again throughout this module. iv. What happens when the context window is full? Reaching the 200,000-token limit doesn't stop Bob or throw an error. Instead, a new conversation starts automatically in the background. Bob generates a summary of the previous conversation or session, and then that summary is pre-pended as context to the new conversation. Bob will carry on its responses and workflow seamlessly. The process is invisible to you — but it has real consequences for quality and cost, and that is precisely why it's worth understanding how to govern this resource allocation in detail. The first cost: summarization is lossy. When a conversation overflows the context window size and needs to be summarized, the precision and fidelity of the original conversation are compromised. Specific technical details, intermediate reasoning, and nuanced context can be lost within the new Bob conversation. If a critical constraint or edge case was discussed early on, it may not persist into the summary or new conversation's memory, and as such implementation quality can suffer. The second cost: quality degrades above roughly 100,000 tokens. Models don't hold uniform quality across the full range; as the window fills, responses noticeably decline, particularly past the ~100,000-token mark. A conversation using 50,000 tokens will generally produce better output than one using 180,000, all other things being equal. And because tokens are the unit of consumption (measured in Bob Coins ), longer conversations and larger file reads also simply cost more of the finite context window. Less context used equates both better output and lower costs . iv. Context window strategies: persistent artifacts The most effective way to manage all of this is with persistent artifacts . This strategy and pattern of work can be achieved in a variety of ways. Generally speaking, the most effective route involves breaking complex tasks into smaller, more discrete steps. This is, of course, a balancing act: one of the strengths of large language models (LLM) is being able to chain complex tasks into a single request or line of thought; however, the "art" in good prompting is balancing the complexity of those requests with the context window size available to the LLM. One way to achieve this is having each step in an otherwise-complex workfow produce a saved output (such as a file on disk) and starting a new conversation for each major step with reference to those saved outputs. This keeps conversations and instructions contained in terms of size: no single conversation balloons too large in scale and every important decision is preserved as a durable file that you can point back to later. You have already seen this in action. The seat-class feature from Module 2 was built exactly this way: CONVERSATION TASK OUTPUT 1 Plan the feature seat-class-implementation-plan.md , seat-class-architecture.md 2 Implement based on plan Code changes across frontend, backend, and database The implementation conversation consumed just 88,000 of 200,000 tokens — comfortably within the high quality range —because the two-conversation split kept the planning discussion from competing with the implementation for space. CONTEXT WINDOW GUIDELINES Several practical guidelines to keep in mind as you work with Bob's (and any other LLM's) context window: Start new conversations when you switch tasks (planning shouldn't bleed into implementation) Give preference to direct file references ( @/path/to/file ) over copy & paste from clipboard contents Keep MCP configurations lean, since every server's definitions will ultimately eat into the context window with every invocation Monitor token usage to see which interactions are most expensive and adjust accordingly. v. Key takeaways As of June 2026, Bob's context window is 200,000 tokens (~150,000 words) and every new conversation starts with a full allocation of this 200K capacity Context fills according to a hierarchy: system prompts → mode description → rules → MCP tools → messages → file reads/writes When the context window is exhausted, Bob auto-summarizes and seamlessly creates a new conversation under the covers (but summarization can be lossy) Quality noticeably degrades beyond ~100,000 tokens The persistent artifacts pattern ( plan → save → new conversation → implement ) is the primary strategy for managing context The less context window that is consumed, the higher quality of outputs and the lower costs for generation In the following section, you will step away from theory (and the Bob IDE altogether) to go hands-on with the Bob Shell programmatic interface.

At the start of every conversation, content loads in a predictable sequence: ORDER OF OPERATIONS CONTENT NOTES 1 Bob system prompt Hidden from the user; contains Bob's core instructions 2 Mode description The definition of the currently active Bob Mode ( Code , Plan , Custom , etc.) 3 Rules Content from all files in .bob/rules/ 4 MCP tool definitions Can be very large, depending on the number and complexity of connected MCP servers 5 Conversation messages User prompts and Bob's responses 6 File reads and writes Contents of files Bob reads or produces during the conversation THE IMPORTANCE OF GOVERNANCE MCP tool definitions deserve special attention. The more external servers connected via MCP to Bob, the more rapidly that a significant slice of Bob's context window is exhausted before the user (you) send even a single message. This is why the importance of good governance and planning are emphasized again and again throughout this module.
docs.title: iii. What is a context window?

docs.text: Reaching the 200,000-token limit doesn't stop Bob or throw an error. Instead, a new conversation starts automatically in the background. Bob generates a summary of the previous conversation or session, and then that summary is pre-pended as context to the new conversation. Bob will carry on its responses and workflow seamlessly. The process is invisible to you — but it has real consequences for quality and cost, and that is precisely why it's worth understanding how to govern this resource allocation in detail. The first cost: summarization is lossy. When a conversation overflows the context window size and needs to be summarized, the precision and fidelity of the original conversation are compromised. Specific technical details, intermediate reasoning, and nuanced context can be lost within the new Bob conversation. If a critical constraint or edge case was discussed early on, it may not persist into the summary or new conversation's memory, and as such implementation quality can suffer. The second cost: quality degrades above roughly 100,000 tokens. Models don't hold uniform quality across the full range; as the window fills, responses noticeably decline, particularly past the ~100,000-token mark. A conversation using 50,000 tokens will generally produce better output than one using 180,000, all other things being equal. And because tokens are the unit of consumption (measured in Bob Coins ), longer conversations and larger file reads also simply cost more of the finite context window. Less context used equates both better output and lower costs .
docs.title: iv. What happens when the context window is full?

docs.text: The most effective way to manage all of this is with persistent artifacts . This strategy and pattern of work can be achieved in a variety of ways. Generally speaking, the most effective route involves breaking complex tasks into smaller, more discrete steps. This is, of course, a balancing act: one of the strengths of large language models (LLM) is being able to chain complex tasks into a single request or line of thought; however, the "art" in good prompting is balancing the complexity of those requests with the context window size available to the LLM. One way to achieve this is having each step in an otherwise-complex workfow produce a saved output (such as a file on disk) and starting a new conversation for each major step with reference to those saved outputs. This keeps conversations and instructions contained in terms of size: no single conversation balloons too large in scale and every important decision is preserved as a durable file that you can point back to later. You have already seen this in action. The seat-class feature from Module 2 was built exactly this way: CONVERSATION TASK OUTPUT 1 Plan the feature seat-class-implementation-plan.md , seat-class-architecture.md 2 Implement based on plan Code changes across frontend, backend, and database The implementation conversation consumed just 88,000 of 200,000 tokens — comfortably within the high quality range —because the two-conversation split kept the planning discussion from competing with the implementation for space. CONTEXT WINDOW GUIDELINES Several practical guidelines to keep in mind as you work with Bob's (and any other LLM's) context window: Start new conversations when you switch tasks (planning shouldn't bleed into implementation) Give preference to direct file references ( @/path/to/file ) over copy & paste from clipboard contents Keep MCP configurations lean, since every server's definitions will ultimately eat into the context window with every invocation Monitor token usage to see which interactions are most expensive and adjust accordingly.
docs.title: iv. Context window strategies: persistent artifacts

docs.text: As of June 2026, Bob's context window is 200,000 tokens (~150,000 words) and every new conversation starts with a full allocation of this 200K capacity Context fills according to a hierarchy: system prompts → mode description → rules → MCP tools → messages → file reads/writes When the context window is exhausted, Bob auto-summarizes and seamlessly creates a new conversation under the covers (but summarization can be lossy) Quality noticeably degrades beyond ~100,000 tokens The persistent artifacts pattern ( plan → save → new conversation → implement ) is the primary strategy for managing context The less context window that is consumed, the higher quality of outputs and the lower costs for generation In the following section, you will step away from theory (and the Bob IDE altogether) to go hands-on with the Bob Shell programmatic interface.

docs.text: MODULE 4 | SCALE & EXTEND BOB SHELL i. Moving beyond the IDE Everything so far has lived inside the IDE. Bob Shell brings the same core capabilities to a terminal — a keyboard-driven, command-line form factor installed separately from the VS Code extension and runnable in any standard terminal. For developers who live in the terminal, it unlocks workflows that are difficult or impossible in the IDE: headless automation, scripting, and running several Bob instances in parallel. This is what taking Bob to enterprise scale looks like in practice. Watch first: Chapter 4.2: Bob Shell [IBM Bob L3] Maximilian Jesch (Outbound Product Manager — IBM Bob) showcases how to work with Bob's shell and shell commands. [4 min] ADDITIONAL DOCUMENTATION Heads-up: completing this lesson may require additional guidance from IBM Bob's full product documentation to install Bob Shell. Detailed documentation is available from IBM.com ii. Why this matters The Bob IDE and Bob Shell are complementary vectors for working with IBM Bob. In practice, you will discover that many workflows run both the Bob IDE and Bob Shell side-by-side. Some additional points of comparison on where and when to leverage either (or both) interfaces: USE CASE BOB IDE BOB SHELL Visual file exploration Better Limited Keyboard-driven workflows Good Excellent Automation and scripting Not supported Supported (headless mode) Parallel instances Difficult Trivial Getting started Easier Steeper learning curve iii. Three reasons to reach for Bob Shell Keyboard efficiency. Bob Shell removes mouse-driven interaction entirely — navigating files, issuing commands, reviewing output, and prompting Bob all happen through the keyboard. For developers who have internalized terminal workflows, the path from thought to action is faster, and the efficiency compounds; many adopt Bob Shell as a full daily-driver replacement for the IDE once it's familiar. Parallelization. Because Bob Shell runs in a terminal, multiple independent instances can run at once — one per tab, pane, or multiplexer window — which is trivial to set up compared with any IDE-based approach. You might run the IDE sidebar for exploratory work while one shell instance implements a backend change, another writes tests for a separate component, and a third generates documentation. Tasks with no shared state are the ideal candidates. Headless mode. Bob Shell supports a headless mode where input is piped directly to Bob rather than entered interactively. This single capability turns Bob into a programmable component rather than just an interactive assistant. Pipe compiler output to it for diagnosis, pipe log files to it for incident triage, generate summaries or reports as part of a script, or let it attempt minor fixes autonomously and escalate the complex ones. For example: cat error.log | bob "explain this" A NOTE ON SAFETY Governance, as always, is paramount. By default, Bob Shell applies stricter auto-approval settings than the Bob IDE. For example, file writes and shell commands require explicit confirmation by the user. The stricter default behavior is deliberate given that Bob Shell is often used in environments (servers, continuous integration pipelines, or scripts) where unreviewed changes can carry broader consequences, compared to within the constraints of a local IDE session. iv. Getting started and navigation tips Once installed, invoke Bob Shell by running: bob On first use, Shell prompts for IBM login credentials. After successfully authenticating, it behaves much like the Bob IDE Chat interface: you type natural-language prompts directly at into the Shell prompt, with Bob reading and modifying files in the current working directory based upon those requests. INVOKING REGULAR (NON-BOB) SHELL COMMANDS Within a Bob Shell session, prefix any command with ! to invoke regular (non-Bob) shell commands. For example: !git diff !cat README.md !ls -la The net result for the developer (you) is being able to alternate between AI-assisted workflows (with Bob Shell ) and standard bash shell operations seamlessly, without needing to leave or create a separate session. v. Hands-on: Installing and using Bob Shell Follow the video for a full walkthrough: Chapter 4.2: Bob Shell [IBM Bob L3] To begin, you will first need to follow the directions below for setting up Bob Shell within your Windows or MacOS environment. Follow the instruction set specific to your operating system. Afterwards, you will go hands-on with using Bob Shell to programmatically send a prompt, drop into Shell Mode, and explore various commands. Open a new Terminal window by pressing the Terminal button at the top of Bob IDE. Alternatively, you can use the Terminal application on MacOS or the PowerShell application on Windows. Click New Terminal to launch a new console instance. To download the Bob Shell to your local machine, follow the instruction set below that matches your machine's operating system. MAC OR LINUX Copy the following command and paste into the Terminal console, then hit Enter to execute: curl -fsSL https://bob.ibm.com/download/bobshell.sh | sudo bash You will be prompted for your machine's system password to complete the install. For security, no characters appear on screen as you type — but your input is being registered. Wait for the Terminal console to report back a successful installation of the Bob Shell. The message should look similar to the following: bobshell x.x.x has been succesfully installed You can now run: bob When ready, proceed to Step 4 . WINDOWS OS Copy the following command and paste into the PowerShell console, then hit Enter to execute: powershell -ep Bypass 'irm -Uri "https://bob.ibm.com/download/bobshell.ps1" | iex' Wait for the PowerShell console to report back a successful installation of the Bob Shell. The message should look similar to the following: bobshell x.x.x has been succesfully installed You can now run: bob When ready, proceed to Step 4 . With the Bob Shell now successfully installed, copy and paste the following instruction into the console and hit Enter : bob The console will launch an external "Log in to IBM" page via your web browser. Complete the SSO sign-in using your w3ID credentials (also tied to your IBM Bob account.) Once signed in, you will be redirected to an "Authentication Successful!" page. You may safely close the web browser at this time. If this is your first time using Bob Shell , there's a small amount of configuration and bookkeeping to do beforehand. If prompted to accept the license agreement , review the contents and then type Y (followed by Enter ) if you agree to the terms and conditions. When prompted to connect the Bob IDE to Bob Shell , use the arrow keys to highlight option 1. Yes (or type 1 ), and then press Enter to execute the command. ERROR: Failed to automatically enable IDE integration... If you receive this error: Locate the currently-running process within the Terminal sidebar and press the bin icon to terminate it Create a new Terminal console selecting Terminal > New Terminal from the top-line menu bar Return to Step 4 and execute the steps a second time Within the Terminal console, a Welcome to Bob Shell splash screen will appear to confirm a successful connection has been established to the service. Scroll down until you reach the input field , denoted by the > ("greater than") brace. To test functionality, copy and paste the following prompt into the input field, then hit Enter to execute: check the readme and see if you can make any improvements In the same way that it did using the Agentic Sidebar within the Bob IDE, the Bob Shell narrates its progression through a Todo List as it executes upon the work. Occasionally, Bob will ask for approval to complete tasks or actions as operates The difference with Bob Shell is such check-ins with the human-in-the-loop happen via the Terminal console If asked for approvals, Bob Shell will present you with a numerated list as you saw previously. Either use the arrows on your keyboard to move up and down the list, or press the corresponding number on your keyboard, to highlight one of the options Confirm the selection by hitting Enter Recommended that in all cases (for the hands-on lab) you opt for: 1. Yes, allow once The diff view captured in the screenshot below highlights Bob's proposed updates to the README.md file. As before: red highlights denote content marked for removal; green highlights denote content scheduled to be added. Prefixing any input into the Bob Shell console with an exclamation mark ! drops Bob Shell into shell mode (akin to a bash shell), where you can run ordinary shell commands. Test this by copy and pasting the following command into the Terminal console, then hit Enter to execute. !cat readme The cat (concatenate) command is used to view, create, and combine file contents directly from the console. As a result of executing the cat command, the Terminal console simply prints the README.md contents to the window. EXITING ! SHELL MODE Note that the ! exclamation marker remains on the left-hand side of the Terminal console. This indicates that the console remains in the generic shell mode . To exit generic shell mode, and return to the Bob Shell , press Esc at any time. Next, try using the git diff ... command to compare differences across the working copy of README.md (on your machine) and the version tracked within the local Git repository (typically the last commit.) Copy and paste the following instruction into the console, then press Enter to execute. git diff README.md Take note of the + and - symbols on the left-side edge of each line: these denote changed lines between the two versions (indicating a new line added or existing line removed , respectively.) To exit generic shell mode, and return to the Bob Shell , press Esc at any time. Press Esc now to return to the Bob Shell , where you will investigate more of the commands available before progressing to the next chapter. There are a multitude of commands and operations you can perform using the Bob Shell , which we have just barely scratched the surface of here. Copy and paste the following command, followed by Enter , to display a full list of ways that you can interact with the Bob Shell : /help vi. Key takeaways Bob Shell provides the same capabilities as Bob IDE, but via a programmatic console Invoke the Bob Shell with bob ; use the ! prefix for normal shell commands within a session Exit the normal shell ( ! ) shell mode and return to Bob Shell by typing Esc Auto-approval is strict by default in Bob Shell , requiring you to confirm actions as prompted CORE BENEFITS OF BOB SHELL Keyboard efficiency: faster for Terminal-native developers once the interface is learned Headless mode: cat file | bob "prompt" enables automation, pipeline integration, and scripted workflows Parallelization: multiple Bob Shell instances can run simultaneously for independent tasks To conclude the hands-on modules, you will next examine Bob's open standards Model Context Protocol (MCP) as a means for connecting Bob to everything else within your enterprise.

docs.text: MODULE 4 | SCALE & EXTEND EXTENDING WITH MCP i. Connecting everything back to Bob Watch first: Chapter 5.1: MCP [IBM Bob L3] Maximilian Jesch (Outbound Product Manager — IBM Bob) digs into the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and how it relates to Bob. [5 min] Why this matters A partner that can only touch files and run terminal commands is powerful, but it is still an island. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is what connects Bob to the rest of your world — a standardized interface that lets LLM-powered applications reach external tools, services, and data sources through one consistent integration layer. Add MCP servers to Bob, and its reach extends to any external service that provides one. This is the final move in scaling Bob across an enterprise: making it a participant in the systems your teams already use. THE FULL JOURNEY ALONG THE AI MATURITY CURVE This final module completes your journey along the AI Maturity Curve . Before continuing on, step back and look at the shape of what you've done: - You began with Bob finishing your lines and predicting your next edit (Module 1 | Assist) - You handed Bob whole features to build from an approved plan (Module 2 | Delegate) - You taught Bob about your project structure and your organization's standards, reinforcing that learning until Bob behaved like a teammate (Module 3 | Tailor) - Finally, you made Made reliable at scale and connected to the systems your enterprise already runs (Module 4 | Scale & Extend) A common thread across all of these modules and discussions has been the core value that the developer stays in control. Only the stakes changed (and escalated) across the journey from the nascent phases to the right-most portions of the curve. At Assist , control was apparent — the user (you) accepting each suggestion in sequence with a high degree of oversight. At Delegate , it was approving the plans that Bob put in place and trusting it to carry on the work beyond that point. At Tailor , it was encoding the rules and committing them to repositories that would ensure Bob adhered to your coding and organizational standards. Currently, at the Scale & Extend phase, trust becomes more about governing context, credentials, and tool access. Follow this progression with any conversation or demonstration you have with clients about IBM Bob. Don't limit your planning to only a parade of features. Build out the storyline presented here to demonstrate a trustworthy path by which a team grows into working with an AI partner, without ever feeling like they've relinquished control or made shortcuts to their organization's established ways of winning. What MCP is MCP defines a standard interface for connecting LLM applications to external systems. Before it existed, wiring an LLM to an external tool meant building a custom connection layer for each one — a significant, inconsistent effort that varied across teams and organizations. MCP replaces that with a single protocol both sides implement: once a service offers an MCP server, any MCP-compatible client (Bob included) can connect to it immediately, with no custom integration work. A coordination innovation, not just a technical one MCP originated at Anthropic and has since been transferred to the Linux Foundation , making it a vendor-neutral, openly governed standard — and that governance is what accelerated its adoption. Most major external services and developer tools now ship MCP servers, creating an extensive ecosystem of ready-to-use integrations. MCP's real impact isn't primarily technical — it's a coordination innovation. A shared standard eliminated duplicated integration effort across the whole industry. Adding an MCP server MCP servers are configured in Bob's settings through a JSON configuration file. The flow is: open Bob settings via the three-dot menu (⋯), navigate to MCP Servers , add the server configuration in JSON, and supply credentials as required. Most services publish their configuration snippet in their official documentation — and Bob itself can insert the JSON for you, handling indentation and brackets automatically. How you handle credentials is a governance decision in itself: Method Description Best for Inline in config Personal access token written directly in the JSON file Quick setup, local development only Environment variable Token stored as an OS environment variable, referenced in config Cleaner setup, avoids token in config file Context Forage Open-source MCP gateway for managing complex, multi-server setups Teams, production environments, multiple credentials Using MCP tools MCP tools are available only in Advanced mode . With Advanced mode active, Bob automatically recognizes the tools exposed by every configured server and invokes them in response to natural-language requests — no special syntax required. Bob simply decides which MCP tools to call based on the task you describe. An example: the GitHub MCP server The GitHub MCP server shows how much a single integration can add. Configure it — paste GitHub's configuration snippet into the JSON config, then add a personal access token whose permissions match the operations Bob will perform (reading issues, creating commits, adding comments, closing issues) — and with Advanced mode active, Bob can list and read issues, create commits and push changes, add comments, close issues, and link commits to issues. A token with insufficient permissions will simply cause the affected operation to fail, and Bob will report the permission error so you can update the token. Strung together, those capabilities make a complete issue-resolution loop possible entirely through natural language: ask Bob to list open issues (it calls the GitHub MCP tool to retrieve them), describe the one to fix (Bob reads the relevant code and implements the change), instruct it to commit and push (it calls the right MCP tools and git commands), then have it comment on the issue with a link to the commit and close it. A full development cycle — from issue to closed resolution — without ever leaving the Bob interface. And GitHub is just one server in a fast-growing ecosystem that already spans version-control and code-review platforms, project-management and issue-tracking tools, databases and data services, cloud-infrastructure providers, and internal enterprise systems. In practice, most of the external integrations a development team relies on can be connected to Bob through MCP, with no custom development. Hands-on (optional): the GitHub MCP server Follow the video for a full walkthrough of this scenario: Chapter 5.1: MCP [IBM Bob L3] The following walkthrough connects the GitHub MCP server end to end. Note that it is entirely optional — you're welcome to simply read through it rather than perform the steps, especially since it involves creating a credential. THIS MCP SECTION IS OPTIONAL! You can simply read through the steps to complete this - you do not need to take action or actually proceed through these steps. \ \ This optional section is subject to change. Validate the current GitHub MCP server steps against the latest product and provider documentation before attempting to implement this with clients. Navigate to the following page: https://github.com/github/github-mcp-server Scroll down to the "Local GitHub MCP Server" section and click the hyperlink: Create a GitHub Personal Access Token Create a GitHub account (or sign in). You'll need a GitHub Personal Access Token for this section. After signing in, you're redirected to the token-creation page. Give the token any name you like — we used IBM Bob . Leave the other fields at their defaults and scroll down to press Generate token . Click Generate token again on the pop-up that appears. We are redirected to this page with our github PAT. Copy this to another document - ideally a secure password manager. For ease of use, we will store it in plaintext document (Notepad) for now, but this is a bad practice for security overall. Remember - this section is optional - so you don't actually need to perform these steps if you have security concerns, Paste your GitHub PAT in your secure password manager (or, less securely, in a plaintext document like Notepad). If you ( optionally ) choose to work through this section, you will require the PAT you record here. Click the three dots ( ... ) in the top corner of the agentic sidebar. Click MCP Servers . Click Open next to Project MCPs. Expand the Modes button. Under modes, select 🛠️ Advanced — this unlocks MCP tools. We'll configure the MCP server right from the agentic sidebar. docs.text: A partner that can only touch files and run terminal commands is powerful, but it is still an island. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is what connects Bob to the rest of your world — a standardized interface that lets LLM-powered applications reach external tools, services, and data sources through one consistent integration layer. Add MCP servers to Bob, and its reach extends to any external service that provides one. This is the final move in scaling Bob across an enterprise: making it a participant in the systems your teams already use. THE FULL JOURNEY ALONG THE AI MATURITY CURVE This final module completes your journey along the AI Maturity Curve . Before continuing on, step back and look at the shape of what you've done: - You began with Bob finishing your lines and predicting your next edit (Module 1 | Assist) - You handed Bob whole features to build from an approved plan (Module 2 | Delegate) - You taught Bob about your project structure and your organization's standards, reinforcing that learning until Bob behaved like a teammate (Module 3 | Tailor) - Finally, you made Made reliable at scale and connected to the systems your enterprise already runs (Module 4 | Scale & Extend) A common thread across all of these modules and discussions has been the core value that the developer stays in control. Only the stakes changed (and escalated) across the journey from the nascent phases to the right-most portions of the curve. At Assist , control was apparent — the user (you) accepting each suggestion in sequence with a high degree of oversight. At Delegate , it was approving the plans that Bob put in place and trusting it to carry on the work beyond that point. At Tailor , it was encoding the rules and committing them to repositories that would ensure Bob adhered to your coding and organizational standards. Currently, at the Scale & Extend phase, trust becomes more about governing context, credentials, and tool access. Follow this progression with any conversation or demonstration you have with clients about IBM Bob. Don't limit your planning to only a parade of features. Build out the storyline presented here to demonstrate a trustworthy path by which a team grows into working with an AI partner, without ever feeling like they've relinquished control or made shortcuts to their organization's established ways of winning.
docs.title: Why this matters

docs.text: MCP defines a standard interface for connecting LLM applications to external systems. Before it existed, wiring an LLM to an external tool meant building a custom connection layer for each one — a significant, inconsistent effort that varied across teams and organizations. MCP replaces that with a single protocol both sides implement: once a service offers an MCP server, any MCP-compatible client (Bob included) can connect to it immediately, with no custom integration work.
docs.title: What MCP is

docs.text: MCP originated at Anthropic and has since been transferred to the Linux Foundation , making it a vendor-neutral, openly governed standard — and that governance is what accelerated its adoption. Most major external services and developer tools now ship MCP servers, creating an extensive ecosystem of ready-to-use integrations. MCP's real impact isn't primarily technical — it's a coordination innovation. A shared standard eliminated duplicated integration effort across the whole industry.
docs.title: A coordination innovation, not just a technical one

docs.text: MCP servers are configured in Bob's settings through a JSON configuration file. The flow is: open Bob settings via the three-dot menu (⋯), navigate to MCP Servers , add the server configuration in JSON, and supply credentials as required. Most services publish their configuration snippet in their official documentation — and Bob itself can insert the JSON for you, handling indentation and brackets automatically. How you handle credentials is a governance decision in itself: Method Description Best for Inline in config Personal access token written directly in the JSON file Quick setup, local development only Environment variable Token stored as an OS environment variable, referenced in config Cleaner setup, avoids token in config file Context Forage Open-source MCP gateway for managing complex, multi-server setups Teams, production environments, multiple credentials

docs.text: MCP tools are available only in Advanced mode . Bob simply decides which MCP tools to call based on the task you describe.

docs.text: The GitHub MCP server shows how much a single integration can add. Configure it — paste GitHub's configuration snippet into the JSON config, then add a personal access token whose permissions match the operations Bob will perform (reading issues, creating commits, adding comments, closing issues) — and with Advanced mode active, Bob can list and read issues, create commits and push changes, add comments, close issues, and link commits to issues. A token with insufficient permissions will simply cause the affected operation to fail, and Bob will report the permission error so you can update the token. Strung together, those capabilities make a complete issue-resolution loop possible entirely through natural language: ask Bob to list open issues (it calls the GitHub MCP tool to retrieve them), describe the one to fix (Bob reads the relevant code and implements the change), instruct it to commit and push (it calls the right MCP tools and git commands), then have it comment on the issue with a link to the commit and close it. A full development cycle — from issue to closed resolution — without ever leaving the Bob interface. And GitHub is just one server in a fast-growing ecosystem that already spans version-control and code-review platforms, project-management and issue-tracking tools, databases and data services, cloud-infrastructure providers, and internal enterprise systems. In practice, most of the external integrations a development team relies on can be connected to Bob through MCP, with no custom development.

docs.text: MODULE 3 | TAILOR /INIT AND AGENTS.MD i. Teaching Bob your codebase Across the first two modules ( Assist and Delegate ), Bob was put to work with minimal-to-no background or context about your codebase. Bob proved itself to be capable, but operating and working only from what it could read and infer based in the moment. Module 3 ( Tailor ) will change that approach markedly. Here you will teach Bob about your project and your standards, so that Bob begins behaving like a teammate who already knows how your team works. There are three ways to tailor Bob which build on one another: Provide Bob with durable knowledge about your codebase (so it stops rediscovering your project from scratch with every invocation) Encode the standards Bob must always follow (so quality and conventions are enforced without needing to be re-typed) Shape Bob's behavior to fit each role on your team (so a product manager and a senior engineer each get the specialized version of Bob that they need). AI MATURITY CURVE Notice where control lives at this stage in the AI Maturity Curve . Whereas in Modules 1 and 2 you approved Bob's work as it happened, here in Module 3 you write the rules down — commit them to the repository —and have them applied automatically, every time, for everyone. Viewed another way: Bob, at this stage in your jouney, has progressed beyond delegated work towards tailored work. Bob's behaviors, capabilities, and understanding are now being attuned specifically to the workflow and personas engaging with it. ii. Why this matters Watch first: Chapter 3.1: init Command [IBM Bob L3] Maximilian Jesch (Outbound Product Manager — IBM Bob) shows how Bob's init command summarizes a large, complex codebase. [2 min] Large language models (LLM) are stateless and therefore every new conversation, without intervening strategies or techniques, will begin with no memory of the last interaction. Left to its own devices, Bob would need to rediscover your codebase from scratch at the start of each interaction — an inefficient approach for a small project and an impractically cumbersome approach for a large one. The /init command solves this challenge. It scans your project and generates a structured summary that Bob loads as persistent context for every new conversation. The /init command thus becomes the primary mechanism for giving Bob durable knowledge of your project's structure, conventions, and code. All without needing to re-read every file with each new invocation. RUNNING /init Initializing a project's context takes seconds and requires no additional configuration. To do so using IBM Bob: Open the agentic sidebar in Bob IDE Enter the slash command: /init Bob reads the relevant files in the project Bob generates the agents.md context file You'll have plenty of opportunities to practice this yourself when the hands-on portion of Module 3 kicks off. Beforehand, however, it's important to understand more about the complementary agents.md file. THE AGENTS.MD FILE The primary output of the /init command is agents.md : a plain-text Markdown file placed in the project root directory. Think of agents.md as onboarding documentation written for specifically for Bob. It provides a concise, actionable summary of everything Bob needs to understand about the project in order to work effectively with it. The documentation typically covers: the project's overview and purpose; its directory structure and key file locations; the technology stack and dependencies; architectural patterns and conventions; and development workflows. From the point it is first introduced and defined, agents.md is automatically prepended to every new conversation a user has with Bob, ensuring the LLM has immediate project context without requiring any manual file read efforts. MODE-SPECIFIC CONTEXT FILES Alongside the main agents.md Markdown documentation, the /init command also generates context files tuned to each one of Bob's built-in Modes (which we examined in Module 2 ): FILE MODE .bob/agents.md All conversations (global project context) .bob/agents-code.md Code mode .bob/agents-plan.md Plan mode .bob/agents-ask.md Ask mode .bob/agents-advanced.md Advanced mode Each mode-specific file extends the base context with what matters most for the successful operations of a given Mode. Context for Plan mode might emphasize architectural conventions, while Code mode context would benefit from highlighting file structure and naming patterns. iii. Hands-on: generating your project context Follow the video for a full walkthrough: Chapter 3.1: init Command [IBM Bob L3] The larger your codebase, the more valuable a well-maintained agents.md asset becomes. On a small project, Bob could conceivably read every file each conversation; even so, having a pre-defined agents.md is still more efficient than the read-everything alternative. On a large project, an agents.md manifest becomes the backbone of the entire workflow. It provides detailed guidance for how Bob should navigate the codebase, without exhausting the context window on file reads. TIPS FOR /INIT AND AGENTS.MD Execute the /init command after significant changes to ensure Bob picks up on any new modules or services, restructured directory trees, new framework, and so on. If there are instances where you (the administrator) want to capture context without performing an automated scan— or believe that an automated scan might miss some key elements, such as business rules or deployment conventions —then you may also edit the agents.md asset by-hand. Let's give Bob durable knowledge of the Galaxium Travels codebase by running the /init command and generating its agents.md files. First, ensure that Bob has enabled Code mode within the Agentic Sidebar. Within the Agentic Sidebar, type the following: /init Once you have finished typing, you will be presented with a Bob Commands window pop-up with the /init command displayed. Click Send message (the purple button with the arrow) to execute the instruction. Bob will now outline its plan of acton. Review the proposed steps, then click Approve to continue. If you enabled auto-approval in Module 2 , this workflow may complete on its own with no further intervention required on your part. As expected, a To-Do list will appear as Bob begins executing the workflow. Review the steps it proposes be undertaken and press Approve to proceed. Bob may ask you to approve commands such as mkdir , which is necessary in order to create the directories its agents.md file will require. Press the blue Run button to grant such permissions and carry on with the workflow. Likewise, as Bob creates or edits the protected agents.md and related configuration files, you may be asked for further approvals. Press the blue Approve button if prompted to do so. Once Bob has completed the requested workflow, you'll be presented with an "All tasks completed!" message within the agentic sidebar along with several newly-created files: The /init command successfully created a main AGENTS.md file in the project root and mode-specific files in .bob. iv. Key takeaways LLMs are stateless by default: every conversation starts fresh, with no memory of the last session or chat The /init command scans your project(s) and generates agents.md documentation, a context file that will subsequently be included with every new Bob conversation agents.md functions like onboarding documentation: a structured summary that Bob utilizes to navigate your project(s) Mode-specific agents.md files give targeted context for IBM Bob's Code , Plan , Ask , and Advanced modes For large-scale projects, agents.md is essential: Bob cannot feasibly read every file at the start of each conversation without exhausting its (sizeable) context window Re-run the /init command after major changes to capture the latest context for project(s) In the chapter ahead, you will examine strategies for encoding your organization's coding standards using Bob Rules .
